analysis.one_liner: Extends four olestra fat-substitute patents by ten years for their corporate owner.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Judiciary Committee and died without a vote or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Olestra is a man-made fat substitute that was awaiting government approval as a food ingredient. Because that approval process took years, the patents covering it were running out or had already expired. This bill would have used legislation — rather than the normal patent system — to extend or reinstate four specific olestra patents for ten years starting when the government first approved olestra, effectively handing the patent owner a decade-long monopoly on the ingredient.
analysis.who_benefits: The owner of the four named olestra patents — Procter & Gamble, which developed olestra — would gain a government-guaranteed ten-year monopoly on the ingredient for food uses, allowing it to charge licensing fees or premium prices for that entire period. Any snack or food maker wanting to use olestra would have to buy access.

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the terms of four specific United States patents covering olestra, and any reissues of them, by ten years tied to the date of the first federal regulation approving olestra as a food additive.

For patents that had already expired before olestra was approved, the bill would 'reinstitute' them — revive dead patents — for ten years starting at approval, a remedy the normal patent system does not provide.
The extension would be certified by the Commissioner of Patents and Trademarks at the patent owner's request within ninety days of approval, limited to food and food-additive uses of olestra.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, who would face monopoly pricing on olestra-containing foods for a decade, and food manufacturers, who would pay licensing fees to use the ingredient. The public also loses the usual open competition that follows patent expiration.

drawbacks.text: Legislating a private patent extension for named patents removes competition on that ingredient for ten years, keeping prices for olestra-containing products higher than an open market would produce.

The bill would revive patents that had already expired — 'reinstituting' them — which goes beyond the ordinary practice of compensating for regulatory delay and hands the owner exclusive rights on inventions that had entered the public domain.

A fair objection from supporters: the government's own safety-review process consumed years of the patents' life, so an extension partly just compensates the inventor for time lost waiting for FDA approval — the same logic Congress has used for drugs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit flows almost entirely to one company's patent portfolio; the cost is spread thinly across consumers in the form of a decade of monopoly pricing. There is a legitimate argument that a lengthy government approval process warrants some patent-term relief, but this bill was drafted for four named patents rather than as a general rule, which is why it is classified as private legislation.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its intellectual property subcommittee, and died there when the Congress ended without ever reaching a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Willis Gradison of Ohio introduced the bill on June 26, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Judiciary.
Two weeks later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Intellectual Property and Judicial Administration, where it sat for the rest of the 102nd Congress.
No other member cosponsored the bill, and it never received a committee markup or a floor vote before Congress adjourned on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and any competitor in the fat-substitute market are better off, because the ten-year government-granted monopoly on olestra was never enacted. The patent holder, Procter & Gamble, failed to get the extension it sought.

for.name: Rep. Willis Gradison, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the four olestra patents; it drew no cosponsors.

for.name: Procter & Gamble
for.what_they_did: The company whose patented fat substitute the bill was written to protect; its product stood to gain a ten-year monopoly extension.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its intellectual property subcommittee on July 8, 1991, and never scheduled action on it; the bill died in subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member besides the sponsor supported the bill, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have locked in a ten-year exclusive right to olestra for food uses, letting the company charge monopoly prices or licensing fees. Consumer costs are the direct flip side of the company's gain.

They would gain access to a novel fat substitute but only by paying the patent holder during the ten-year extension. Without the extension they would have waited for the patents to lapse and used olestra royalty-free.

industries.industry: Producers of competing fats and fat substitutes
industries.note: A ten-year exclusive extension would have kept a potential blockbuster ingredient off-limits to competitors for a decade, delaying any rival product's market. Its death preserved their competitive position.
